IV. APPLICABILITY EVALUATION
Emotion can inﬂuence one’s behavior and reﬂect one’s health
states to some extent. Thus, an intelligent system capable
of recognizing and interfering one’s emotions can perform
better in the areas where emotion plays a crucial role, such
as intelligent tutoring system, healthcare scenarios, design
and team works, intelligent toys, lie detection and customer
service [3], [51], [76]. To build such affective intelligent
systems, awareness of individual’s emotion is a basic require-
ment. In addition, measuring a system user’s emotion with-
out causing inconvenience to the user is preferred. With
this concern, the researchers [90], [96] proposed to recog-
nize emotions from KMT dynamics. The study [42] also
realized that knowing the user’s emotional states enables
mobile phones to support more intelligent interactions, mak-
ing the devices react/interact more appropriately, naturally,
and friendly with users [76]. There are several applica-
tion areas requiring emotion recognition research with KMT
dynamics (See Table 8). According to Table 8, we will
discuss some popular applications in detail and answer the
RQ 5 and RQ 6.
A. HEALTHCARE
In healthcare area, emotion recognition from KMT dynam-
ics has been applied in detecting Parkinson’s disease and
mood disorder. By predicting emotional states based on
KMT dynamics, the research [82] showed a potential for
exploiting biometric data in the healthcare-oriented domain.
In [53], the idea of early identiﬁcation of Parkinson’s disease
through behavioral data from smartphone was tested, both
emotional and physical states were analyzed for monitoring
ageing pathology cases like Parkinson’s disease, based on the
i-PROGNOSIS project. The research [104] also proved that
using keystrokes under emotional stimuli is an effective and
intelligent way to detect onset of Parkinson’s disease. For
predicting mood disorder through emotion prediction based
on keyboard data, the research [41] proved that it is feasible
and effective to predict presence and severity of mood dis-
turbance, pointing to the potential of medical treatment for
mood disorders.
B. EDUCATION
It has been proved that emotion has a signiﬁcant effect
on learning outcomes [105]. Keyboard and mouse are the
most common input devices in learning context and collect-
ing data from these devices is widely considered as non-
intrusive, so using KMT dynamics features to investigate the
learners’ emotional states in educational scenario has been
a simple and effective way [87], [92], [94]. In this ﬁeld, the
research [54] proposed to recognize emotions of learners who
learnt English as a second language for improving learning
performance. The study [79] also believed that learners’ per-
formance could be affected by their emotions. Thus, it is
important to build a modern Intelligent ITS which is capa-
ble of recognizing learners’ emotional states and adjusting
learning content accordingly. While the emotion recognition

D. USER AUTHENTICATION
In fact, keystroke dynamics was studied, widely used, and
rapidly developed as a nature choice and complementary
method in user authentication over the last 50 years [48],
[107]–[109]. This can be very practical because it has been
proved that each user has a unique style when they type
through keyboard [109]. More speciﬁcally, the time interval
of successive keystroke, keystroke duration, key pressure or
some other keystroke factors can be used to build up a unique
signature for a user [108]. The study [38] proposed a biologic
veriﬁcation method based on pressure sensor equipped key-

password authentication. By conducting two experiments, the

continuously authenticate users after login authorization, the
study [48] proposed a user-adaptive feature extraction method
to collect keystroke dynamics from free typing text.

mobile phones, the study [40] focused on using touchscreen
data for this purpose. It performed a large-scale study which
showed that a speciﬁc user can be identiﬁed in 5 users with a
relatively high precision. From the result, the conclusion has
been made that touchscreen input patterns are distinguish-
ing for each person. Also based on mobile touchscreen, the
study [39] identiﬁed users almost immediately based on the
way they performed while maintained users’ convenience.

V. GAPS AND FUTURE WORK
Through this systematic analysis of the related work in emo-
tion recognition based on KMT dynamics, some research
gaps are identiﬁed. In this section, we discuss the following
key research gaps and potential future work.
A. BUILDING A COMMON DATASET
Many researchers have investigated emotion recognition
from KMT dynamics, and some of them reached a high
accuracy, but it is meaningless to compare each of them
since there is no common dataset as benchmark for compari-
son [49], [93]. This need was identiﬁed in 2009 [93] but still
not be met yet [49]. The datasets used in literatures are usually
built by individual research groups and the features contained
in different datasets are either diverse or organized in different
formations [104], making them difﬁcult for using as bench-
mark. In addition, emotional states that have been recognized
are also very diverse. For example, some researchers cared
about happiness and sadness [76] while others about arousal
and valence [78]. Thus, it is necessary to build a common
dataset in the future for the purpose of comparing different
algorithms. As for what features should be contained in this
dataset, further work is needed to identify which features
play a more signiﬁcant role in KMT dynamics-based emotion
recognition.
B. CONSIDERING USER FEATURES
User features such as age, gender, culture context, com-
puter proﬁciency, some habits like left-handedness or even
the body postures may also have impact on typing behav-
ior [6], [78]. Ignoring these features may result in a wrong
classiﬁcation. However, most existing studies did not con-
sider user features when building their own dataset. Besides,
other factors come from the devices (e.g. the keyboard layout,
the distance between keyboard and hands) are also important
factors that may change participants’ typing habits. Thus,
using these elements as a supplement of KMT features may
improve the recognition accuracy. In future work, more stud-
ies are needed to explore how to incorporate users features
into the emotion recognition.
C. ASSESSING RECOGNITION PERFORMANCE USING
BIOLOGICAL SIGNALS
Almost all the above research relies on self-reporting for
the assessment of emotion recognition. In these studies, par-
ticipants were requested to record their emotional states in
the form of self-deﬁned questionnaire or Self-Assessment-
Manikin (SAM) questionnaire [92]. This method forces par-
ticipants to break their typing behavior, which defeats the pur-
pose of using keystroke dynamics as a non-intrusive method
to recognize emotions. On the other hand, it is hard to
record participants’ every emotional state accurately, espe-
cially when the limited options of questionnaire do not con-
tain their subtle emotions, or they are even not sure how to
describe their emotions [6]. The biological signals are much
more objective and precise in terms of reﬂecting people’s
emotional states [6], [111], [112]. For example, for those who
do not like to show their emotions, recognizing their emotions
through appearance or behavior habits would be deceptive.
On the contrary, biological features like EEG signals could
still reﬂect real emotion changes. Therefore, in the future,
using biological signals as ground truth in parallel to the KMT
dynamics should be a potential method that improves training
data quality and help researchers evaluate their algorithm
performance more objectively and accurately.
D. IMPROVING PRIVACY AND SAFETY THROUGH
FEDERATED LEARNING
Another challenge is how to improve the safety of the data and
protect the privacy of users. At present, almost all research
collected rich data including personal information, and then
sent those data to a server or cloud storage devices. This
transmitting increases the risk of privacy information loss or
theft. Thus, how to ensure the security of these private data
is a primary problem that each researcher should consider.
However, it is inadequately addressed in most past research.
As the development of hardware performance, the computers,
mobile phones and wearable devices have growing computa-
tional power, so it is increasingly attractive to store and com-
pute emotion related data locally [113]. Federated learning is
a machine learning setting which aims to train a model in the
case that training data are stored in different remote clients.
Under the federated learning concept, the update of the model
is realized by aggregating all the updates of each device [114].
In future work, applying federated learning technology into
affective computing will be an innovative method for privacy
protection.

emotion recognition. However, there is a real situation that
some people are good at writing in their native language,
but not good at inputting them through keyboard typing (for
example, writing Chinese characters by hands rather than
typing letters through keyboard). In this case, changing typing
input model into writing model can be a convenient solution
for most smart phone users. Thus, learning users’ emotions
when they are writing in a touchscreen through stylus or
ﬁnger rather than typing by a touchscreen keyboard is a
potential research direction.
VI. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we have systematically reviewed emotion
recognition based on the KMT dynamics along the dimen-
sions of emotion elicitation, features, recognition meth-
ods, and applications. Based on these dimensions, we have
answered six research questions which most researchers want
to ask, identiﬁed some key related application ﬁelds, current
research gaps, and future research directions.

Abstract
To understand how individual user features affect one’s emotional changes in response 
to stimuli or changes in a situated external environment, it is necessary to measure how 
user features affect one’s behavioral changes (patterns of changes) in the use of keyboard, 
mouse, and touchscreen devices (KMT dynamics), as the measurable behavioral changes 
are related to both user features and the user’s emotional states. Our central research 
questions are: (1) which user features have a significant impact on behavior such as KMT 
dynamics? (2) how do these user features impact behavior from qualitative and quantita­
tive perspectives? and (3) what is an effective framework to support personalized emotion 
recognition? To answer these questions, we conducted a questionnaire survey with 107 
participants to investigate how, and to what extent, user profile features can influence 
keyboard, mouse, and touchscreen usage in dynamics terms (KMT dynamics). We then 
performed data analysis to explore the relationships between an initial set of user feature 
candidates and an initial set of KMT dynamics feature candidates (12 identified from a 
literature review). Based on the identified relationships, we identified seven important user 
features and seven important KMT dynamics features for further KMT-based emotion 
recognition studies. The seven key user features are: gender, KMT proficiency, language 
proficiency, hand using habit, software proficiency, task urgency, and emotion, while the 
seven important KMT dynamics features are: typing speed, typing error rate, pressure 
value of key/strength of pressing touchscreen, mouse (finger or pencil) movement speed, 
clicking speed, clicking strength, and keystroke speed. Finally, we proposed a new emo­
tion recognition framework incorporating the identified key user and KMT dynamics fea­
tures as a guiding model for further research in this field.

1  Introduction
Behavior and emotion are two different forms of human reactions to external environ­
ments or stimuli [1, 2]. Behavior is more of a physical manifestation, while emotion is 
more inclined to internal cognitive, motivational and subjective elements [3, 4]. The main 
difference between these two forms is that behavior can be more easily measured using tech­
nology [5–8], whereas emotion is difficult to assess directly and is typically inferred from 
changes in a subject’s behavior, such as facial expressions [9, 10], body gestures [11], eye 
movements [12], voice and tone [13], physiological signals [14], and keystroke, mouse, and 
touchscreen (KMT) dynamics [15]. Thus, instead of measuring emotions directly, assess­
ing behavioral changes to infer emotions is a practical and effective approach in the field of 
affective computing [16, 17]. User features, such as gender, age, education level, handed­
ness, and language could introduce bias in emotion recognition based on various indicator 
signals [18–20]. However, most existing research focuses on recognizing emotions from 
various behavioral changes without considering individual user features, which limits their 
ability to provide personalized emotion recognition for individual well-being.
To develop personalized emotion recognition, here we propose an initial framework that 
incorporates user features into the emotion recognition process (see Fig. 1). This frame­
work is partially derived from our previous literature review work [15] and is grounded 
in the established relationship between the mind and behavior [1]. It is well observed that, 
even under the same situation, individuals may exhibit different behavioral and emotional 
responses [21], which are associated with individual differences [22, 23]. That means user

Equation (1) describes the factors that affect behavior, while Eq. (2) explains how to inter­

from behavior changes, personal differences or user features need to be taken into account

be investigated: (1) which user features have a significant impact on behavior such as KMT 
dynamics, (2) how do these user features impact behavior from qualitative and quantitative 
perspectives, and (3) how the initial framework can be refined based on the answers to the 
above questions to guide future research.
Referring to Fig. 1, given a set of measurements on KMT dynamics, some user fea­

impact on the user’s KMT behavior and in reverse analysing KMT dynamics can interpret 
the user profile [35].
Note that this initial framework focuses only on behavior changes related to KMT 
dynamics. The reasons for this focus are as follows. First, facial expressions, body gestures, 
and eye-tracking are external bodily reactions, which are easily observed but can sometimes 
be deceptive [9, 11–13]. Second, physiological signals such as EEG, heart rate, and blood 
pressure are generally more authentic but hard to capture [14]. KMT dynamics refer to 
how individuals interact with KMT devices in their daily life and work [30, 36], and can 
be easily captured via applications or tools running in the background without interrupting 
users’ workflow. Thus, the non-intrusive and unobtrusive nature of KMT dynamics makes 
them a better choice to predict a user’s emotional state while using KMT devices [15, 36]. 
Given this, the present study specifically investigates how individual elementary user fea­
tures impact on KMT dynamics.
Regarding to our first research question, previous studies have demonstrated that sev­
eral user features such as gender, age, handedness, education level, and personality have 
coupled relationships with KMT dynamics [22, 37, 38]. Researchers have also successfully 
predicted these user features from measuring KMT dynamics (patterns of changes) with 
a relatively high accuracy [31, 33, 34, 39–42]. However, additional user features, includ­

This study addresses the research questions by conducting a questionnaire survey with 107

features. Based on the findings, the initial personalized emotion recognition framework is 
updated by incorporating the identified key user and KMT dynamics features, providing 
guidance for future research. The main contributions of this study are as follows:
1.	 Identification of key user features that significantly influence the behavior related to 
KMT devices usage.
2.	 Identification of key KMT dynamics features as important behavioral indicators for 
emotion recognition.
3.	 Understanding of how these user features affect the KMT dynamics features from both 
qualitative and quantitative perspectives.
4.	 A new personalized emotion recognition framework is proposed to integrate the identi­
fied key user and KMT dynamics features into the emotion recognition pipeline.

proposed framework, and some limitations of this study; and Sect. 6 concludes this study.

2.1.1  Gender in relation with KMT dynamics
Gender is the most studied user feature in relation to KMT dynamics. It has been investi­
gated that males and females exhibit different behavior and have significantly different ways 
of expressing emotions [24]. The related work is summarized in Table 1, involving devices, 
KMT dynamics, and gender distinction.
The research in [31] focused on predicting gender, based on average values such as the 
duration of the same key (K1), down-down time between two consecutive keys (K3), and 
typing speed (K6) on a physical keyboard. The study found that typing speed (K6) alone is 
insufficient for accurate gender recognition. Similarly, the research in [42] investigated gen­
der-based differences in typing behavior, including typing speed (K6), latency time (K2), 
density of backspaces (K7), backspace time, chunk length, chunk duration, and density 
of suspension points. These gender-based typing behavior differences were found to be 
consistent across various KMT devices. The differences show that females are more likely 
to type faster with fewer errors, and have shorter latency time, chunk duration, and fewer 
suspension points. The study in [43] identified five mobile typing dynamics features most 
useful for gender classification, which are: edit distance (between user input and displayed 
text), Gyrometer X coordinates, number of backspaces (K7), total keys pressed (K21), and 
Gyrometer Y coordinates. The finding supports the results of [42] that males tend to make 
more typing errors than females.
Several studies [35, 44–46] have also explored gender recognition using KMT dynam­
ics features. However, they did not provide a detailed analysis of which specific features 
are most effective in distinguishing between male and female users. In contrast to these 
findings, the research in [32] concluded that no features are significantly useful for gen­
der prediction. These inconsistencies highlight the need for further research to determine 
whether KMT dynamics features can be reliably used for gender prediction, and if so, how 
to identify the most relevant features for this purpose.

2.1.2  Age in relation with KMT dynamics
Age is another most widely studied user feature in relation to KMT dynamics. Table 2 sum­
marizes the relevant studies that focus on age predication using KMT dynamics. These stud­
ies include both qualitative approaches [32, 43] and quantitative analysis [39].
Table 2 shows that typing speed (K6) is regarded as the most important keystroke dynam­
ics for age detection [32, 43]. Young individuals aged 16 to 29 tend to type faster than other 
age groups on both virtual and physical keyboards [32]. In contrast, people over the age of 
30 generally type more slowly, often using only one finger on touchscreen [43]. Teenagers 
aged 10 to 15 may also exhibit slower typing speeds, due to limited experience and skill 
development [32]. A study [39] found a linear relationship, showing that individuals around 
20 years old type 62% faster and have 61% shorter pause times compared to those over 70.
Several other studies have identified a user’s age through KMT dynamics [35, 44–47]; 
however, they provide limited information on which KMT dynamics features are most dis­
tinctive or how different age groups perform differently.
2.1.3  Other user features in relation with KMT dynamics
Some studies have examined other user features such as handedness, education level, num­
ber of hands (fingers) used, and personality. A consistent relationship has been observed in 
studies [41, 48] that individuals tend to (a) type faster on both touchscreen and physical 
keyboards when typing hand matches their handedness, and (b) type more slowly and less 
accurately with their non-dominant hand. Features identified as effective for handedness 
classification include the downtimes of each row’s left and right of the keyboard [41], the 
duration of a single key (K1) and the down-down time between two consecutive keys (K3)

offer the best discriminatory power for handedness identification [45, 49, 50]. Although 
the study [51] used user features such as age and handedness to recognize keystroke pat­

2.2  Research gaps
We summarized the interrelationships among devices, commonly used KMT dynam­
ics features, and recognized user features in Fig. 2. Most studies have identified one 
or more user features using keystroke dynamics [54], whereas mouse dynamics has 
been less frequently explored [32]. Although some studies have used mouse features to 
recognize user gender and age [20, 32], the impact of user features on mouse dynamics 
remains under-investigated. Further research is needed to explore this relationship in 
more depth.
Existing research has studied the correlations between various user features (gender, age, 
handedness, education level, number of hands (fingers) used) and commonly used KMT 
dynamics especially time related features, which are easier to record and measure [45]. In 
the context of education levels recognition, time related keystroke features are also fre­
quently used, but it remains unclear which specific features are more effective. Thus, we 
did not connect education level to any particular feature in Fig. 2. Despite existing research 
efforts, understanding relationships between KMT dynamics and user features requires fur­
ther investigation, as no consensus has been reached from either qualitative or quantitative 
perspectives.
Most notably, none of the aforementioned studies have examined emotion as a user fea­
ture. This clear gap highlights the need for further investigation in this area.

3  Research methodology
This study applies a questionnaire survey covering a broad range of user feature candidates 
and KMT dynamics feature candidates to gain a comprehensive understanding of which 
features are most important in both categories. A questionnaire survey with 107 partici­
pants was conducted to answer the above questions from both qualitative and quantitative 
perspectives. The main steps are (1) to determine what user feature candidates to be inves­
tigated; (2) to define what KMT dynamics feature candidates to be studied; (3) to design 
questionnaire and determine sample size; (4) to validate designed questionnaire with a pilot 
study; (5) to conduct the survey; and (6) to analyse data for drawing conclusions.
3.1  User feature candidates
Building on some previous research [39, 40, 42, 48] that focused on gender, age, handed­
ness, education level, number of hands (fingers) used, and personality, and our previous 
review [15], user feature candidates to be studied in this survey are: (a) Gender, (b) Age, (c) 
Education level, (d) Personality, (e) Language proficiency, (f) Hand using habit when using 
a touchscreen, (g) KMT proficiency/familiarity, (h) Software proficiency, (i) Task urgency, 
and (j) Emotion.
KMT behavior differences across age groups and education levels are mainly caused by 
individuals’ familiarity or proficiency with KMT devices [32, 43]. Therefore, we will anal­
yse the correlations between age and education level with KMT device familiarity, rather 
than directly examining their relationships with KMT dynamics.
Emotion is also an important factor affecting KMT dynamics and can be considered as a 
user feature associated with a user. However, compared to the above user features, emotion 
is a more flexible factor and often changes because of many complex reasons. To make it 
easy to understand the decoupling of emotion with KMT dynamics and other user features, 
this study describes emotion as a kind of dynamic user feature rather than other static fea­
tures listed from a) to i). And in order to signal this dynamic feature out, in Eqs. (1) and (2), 
emotion is separated from the user profile features.

3.4  Distribution and data collection
We launched our questionnaire on the free questionnaire editing and distribution plat­
form  https://www.wjx.cn/, the questionnaire was then distributed online to our research

To ensure the credibility of the analysis results, we first filtered out any invalid responses 
before analysing the answers from participants. We reviewed all 107 responses and con­
firmed that every participant completed the questionnaire. Therefore, all responses were 
valid in this survey.

In the quantitative study, participants’ responses on the questions “what are their perceived 
impact levels” expressed as percentage values, which were used to analyse the overall 
impact levels of each user feature on KMT dynamics. The impact level for each user feature 
was presented as a sliding bar ranging from 0 to 50% in the questionnaire, allowing par­
ticipants to adjust their responses (for example, see Question 14 above). When participants 
selected “no difference” in the last question, the default value for this sliding question was 
set to −3%. The larger the number is, the higher the impact level is. A total of 107 responses 
were recorded for each sliding question, with percentage values ranging from − 3 to 50%. 
The quantitative analysis of these responses provides a general guideline for further study 
to normalize personalised variations in general emotion recognition.

5.1  Important (shortlisted) user features to be included in a user profile description
We shortlist seven important user features from ten user feature candidates based on the

on K18. The estimated overall impact of KMT proficiency on KMT dynamics is 23%. All 
the important user features show at least 16% impact on overall KMT dynamics behavior.

30% impact level.

5.4  Personalized emotion recognition framework
The final identified user features and KMT dynamics features were used to refine the initial 
personalized emotion recognition framework. The updated framework is shown in Fig. 9.
Our personalized emotion recognition framework can provide better guidelines for 
developing emotion recognition systems based on individual user profile that incorporates 
multiple important features. Current emotion recognition methods are often too general and 
less effective when applied across users with differing characteristics. While our frame­
work considers user features, device features, and related behavior features to describe their 
coupling relationships. This integrates emotion generation and emotion recognition into a 
single system structure to provide clear guidelines for realizing personalized emotion rec­
ognition by better understanding of their coupling relationships.
Understanding which user features and how these user features affect KMT dynamics 
will help us integrate user factors into emotion recognition according to the relationship 
framework shown in Fig. 9. Behavior is coupling with stimuli, user features, devices (spe­
cifically for KMT devices), and emotions. Giving the same stimuli and device for every 
user, and after knowing the correlations between user features and behavior, the emotion 
will be recognized by decoupling the function. And the recognition accuracy would be sup­
posed to be higher because every other relevant user factor has been considered.
Figure 9 provides a framework for personalized emotion recognition by understanding 
the relationships among the user features and measurable KMT dynamics behavior. This 
understanding can help filter out influences on measured KMT dynamics (decoupling user

is still not clear.
5.5  Limitations
This study applied a questionnaire survey as the main research methodology. This method is 
suitable to explore the relationships between user features and KMT features in an explain­
able way, since it enables efficient collection of standardised responses from a diverse partic­
ipant pool, ensuring consistency and generalisability in data analysis and findings. However, 
this method may also raise some limitations. First, it has the limited depth of responses. 
Unlike interviews or focus groups, the questionnaire constrained participants’ ability to 
elaborate on their experiences, potentially overlooking nuanced behavioural factors influ­
encing KMD. The second limitation is the self-reported data bias. Participants’ responses 
are subjective, relying on self-perceptions rather than objective measurements, which may 
have introduced bias or inaccuracies. For example, everyone has their own understanding 
about the words like “frequently” and “occasionally”. There is no standard definition for 
each of them, so participants may choose one option just based on their own understanding. 
The third limitation is the lack of contextual understanding. The questionnaire could not 
fully capture workplace dynamics, emotional states, or environmental factors influencing 
KMD, limiting its explanatory power. The fourth limitation is the fixed response options. 
Predefined questions and response categories may have restricted participants’ ability to 
express unique insights, reducing the richness of qualitative data.
6  Conclusion
This study has investigated how and to what extent a user profile feature can influence 
one’s keyboard, mouse, and touch screen usage in KMT dynamics. To achieve this aim, 
we first conducted a questionnaire survey with 107 participants in our qualitative study to 
collect opinion data. Then we performed data analysis to explore the relationships between 
the initial set of user feature candidates and the initial set of KMT dynamics feature can­
didates. We then identified what user features are important to KMT dynamics and in turn 
recognized what KMT dynamics are important for emotion recognition, from their rela­
tionship exploration. As a result, we have found seven important user features which are: 
gender, KMT proficiency, language proficiency, hand using habit, software proficiency, task

firmed as important features for emotion recognition, which are F1, F2, F3, K6, K7, K18, 
and M19. Second, we conducted quantitative analysis of the survey data, and identified to 
which extent (degree) one key user feature could sensibly affect important KMT dynamics 
features. Finally, we updated our emotion recognition framework with identified important 
user features and KMT dynamics features as a future development guidance model for fur­
ther research in the related emotion recognition field.
In summary, this study has made the following contributions:
1.	 Identification of key user features that significantly influence the behavior related to 
KMT devices usage.
2.	 Identification of key KMT dynamics features as important behavioral indicators for 
emotion recognition.
3.	 Understanding of how these user features affect the KMT dynamics features from both 
qualitative and quantitative perspectives.
4.	 A new personalized emotion recognition framework that integrates the identified key 
user and KMT dynamics features into the emotion recognition pipelines.
There are three directions for future work. The first one is to conduct better qualitative study 
with more balanced participants’ profiles. Also, the sample size could be bigger. The second 
direction is to consider more task-related features. Currently, only task urgency has been 
considered. But, in the future, different types of work should be considered. For example, 
some tasks (hard tasks) require higher mental workload, and some (easy tasks) require lower 
mental workload, and in the middle, they are normal daily tasks requiring medium level of 
mental workload. Different tasks require different skills and mental workload; thus, differ­
ent types of tasks may affect KMT dynamics without considering task urgency. And how 
combined features of task urgency and task type affect KMT dynamics features is also 
future research work. And the third direction is to design and develop a digital tool for per­
sonalized emotion recognition to quantitatively evaluate how key user features affect KMT 
behavior and in the reverse direction how to recognize user features such as personality, 
gender, or software proficiency, by detecting user’s emotional states at the same time from 
KMT dynamics features.
